metadata.goal: Analyze how vessels navigate the major bend around southern Langeland in Langelandsbælt, in the southern Great Belt, and identify recurring movement patterns and differences in manoeuvring behaviour.
metadata.dataset_description: Constructed cargo and tanker passages around southern Langeland and into Langelandsbælt, with recurring waterborne turning patterns, phase-dependent speeds, and probabilistic draught-related use of the DW Route Langelandsbaelt.
metadata.source_note: Danish maritime geography is used as context; the visible trajectories and attributes are constructed derived data.
metadata.map_reference_note: The 19 m DW-route centreline is a schematic alignment checked against the Danish Maritime Authority route overview and moving-vessel density from official Danish AIS on 2026-07-21; it is not an ENC boundary. Omø and Agersø outlines are © OpenStreetMap contributors.

insight_list.code:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
df=pd.read_csv(dataset_path); vessels=pd.read_csv(user_dataset_path); trips=df[['trajectory_id','vessel_id','turning_pattern']].drop_duplicates().merge(vessels,on='vessel_id'); trips['draught_group']=np.where(trips.draught_m>=11,'higher draught','lower draught'); print(trips.groupby('draught_group').turning_pattern.value_counts())

insights: Traffic around southern Langeland forms three recurring manoeuvring patterns: an earlier tighter inshore turn, a consistent medium-radius DW-route turn, and a later wider turn on the Route H side.
Larger cargo and tanker vessels typically reduce speed before the main turn, remain slower through the strongest directional change, and gradually recover speed after leaving the bend.
Higher-draught vessels are more likely to follow the more consistent deep-water turning pattern, while lower-draught vessels occupy a broader range of turning paths.
summary: Traffic around southern Langeland forms three recurring manoeuvring patterns: an earlier tighter inshore turn, a consistent medium-radius DW-route turn, and a later wider turn on the Route H side. Larger cargo and tanker vessels typically reduce speed before the main turn, remain slower through the strongest directional change, and gradually recover speed after leaving the bend. Higher-draught vessels are more likely to follow the more consistent deep-water turning pattern, while lower-draught vessels occupy a broader range of turning paths.
